A midnight hour update was made to the bill to try and pull anyone on the fence off to at least let the package move forward. But it wasn’t enough. And negotiations ran until the very end, just before the vote opened. DEMOCRATS HAND TRUMP ONE POWER THEY SPENT YEARS FIGHTING The issues with the package were many and varying among Democrats and Republicans. Several Senate Democrats were not satisfied with the ethics language baked into the Clarity Act that sought to slow the Trump family’s rapidly growing crypto empire. That’s because Trump’s income between 2024 and 2025 erupted by about 250% — from just over $620 million to about $2.2 billion. And much of that increase is attributed to his various holdings and ventures in crypto, which are run by his sons, Don Jr. and Eric, according to the president’s financial disclosure forms reviewed by Fox News Digital. "We could talk a lot about it," Sen. Cory Booker, D-N.J., said of his vote against the bill. "But the simple thing is, it allows the corruption of the president to continue." Sen. Ruben Gallego, D-Ariz., who was working with Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., to strengthen the ethics provision in the package, told Fox News Digital, "We were actually getting very, very close, and at the last minute, the banking staffer from [Sen. Tim] Scott's office came in and just said, ‘negotiations are over.’" "And so, I don't know what happened. You know, we were getting to the point where we were probably going to be able to pass, at least get the motion to proceed, move forward, and then, again, an ethics amendment vote," Gallego said. "But I think they got scared with the fact that they had to take an ethics amendment vote. And that's why they killed it. They pulled it at that last minute, so it's bulls---. We were negotiating at the end. At the end of the day, they cared more about protecting the president's right to grift than trying to get a good bill on digital currency." Others didn’t believe that the language dealing with foreign money laundering had enough teeth. "I have not seen the kind of engagement yet from the Republican side when it comes to countering terrorist financing and cartel financing that would get me to a yes," Sen. Andy Kim, D-N.J., said. "I'm still engaged. I didn't get on board with the GENIUS Act till the very last vote." TRUMP'S $5,000 DIVIDEND CHECKS WOULD COME WITH A MAJOR CATCH UNDER GOP SENATOR'S PLAN Still, some lawmakers argued they should at least move forward with the bill to tweak it as needed. Sen. John Cornyn, R-Texas, was still undecided before the vote. He was worried about how bringing crypto into the fold could affect deposit yields at community banks and guardrails on the currency being "diverted for criminal purposes," but he argued the bill could be strengthened if they moved forward. "What we used to do around here is something called legislate," Cornyn said. "You know where you'd actually vote to get on the bill, but then you amend it, and then you decide whether you're going to support it on the back end." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The bill’s failure does open up the Senate to speedily move to other legislative priorities, like Sen. Ted Cruz's, R-Texas, college sports bill to add protections to student-athletes and slow the big money train ripping through collegiate athletics. "We committed to ensure that we got a vote on college sports," Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., said. "So we'll see if we have 60 [votes]. I don't know the answer for sure to that yet. I hope we do."

articles.title: AfD campaigns using cardboard figures from Hindenburg to Weidel
articles.summary: The parliamentary group of the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) in the Brandenburg state parliament is drawing on the history of the German Empire for...
articles.body:
The Alternative for Germany (AfD) caucus in the Brandenburg state parliament is using cardboard cut-outs of party leaders and historical figures like Otto von Bismarck, Paul von Hindenburg, and Wilhelm II for public events.

The AfD parliamentary group leader Hans-Christoph Berndt emphasized that the use of these figures is not meant to be hero worship, but rather a humorous way for people to take photos with them.

The Brandenburg Office for the Protection of the Constitution has classified the AfD in the state as a far-right extremist organization, a classification that the party is currently appealing in court.

The parliamentary group of the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) in the Brandenburg state parliament is drawing on the history of the German Empire for its public events, using cardboard cut-outs of both party leaders and historical figures.

The life-sized cardboard figures show not only AfD national chairpersons Alice Weidel and Tino Chrupalla, but also historical figures like Reich Chancellor Otto von Bismarck, Reich President Otto von Hindenburg and Emperor Wilhelm II.

From Bismarck to Hindenburg to Wilhelm II

Paul von Hindenburg (1847-1934) was president of the German Reich during the Weimar Republic and is regarded by many as "Hitler's enabler," having appointed him Reich chancellor, thereby paving the way for the dictatorship.

Bismarck (1815-1898) drove forward the founding of the German Empire and introduced social insurance, but took action against the Catholic Church and banned the Social Democratic Party.

Wilhelm II (1859-1941) was the last German Emperor. He contributed to the outbreak of World War I.

Parliamentary group leader: 'No hero worship'

AfD parliamentary group leader Hans-Christoph Berndt warned against what he called "demonizing" historical figures.

"Hindenburg was, after all, the only freely elected president of the German Empire," Berndt said when asked about Hindenburg. He was "certainly someone who contributed greatly to stabilization in the 1920s."

The cardboard cut-outs had been set up with a touch of humour so that people could have their photograph taken with them, he added. "This isn't meant to be hero worship."

The Brandenburg Office for the Protection of the Constitution classifies the AfD in the state as a far-right extremist organization. The party is appealing the classification in court.

articles.title: Russia stages early voting in occupied Ukraine ahead of national election
articles.summary: Russia has begun early voting in its parliamentary elections in Russian-controlled areas of Ukraine’s Donetsk region, with armed personnel accompanying elect...
articles.body:
Mobile polling teams visited homes in rural areas on 14 September, carrying ballot boxes and portable voting booths. Footage showed residents casting their ballots outside their homes, while members of Russia's Central Electoral Commission oversaw the process alongside Russian servicemen and police officers.

Russia's parliamentary election is due to take place nationwide from 18 to 20 September. The Kremlin presents the vote as a measure of public opinion on the war in Ukraine, now in its fifth year. Early voting is also under way in several frontline regions, where Russian authorities say the arrangements are needed to comply with martial law imposed by Moscow and to protect voters and election workers.

In Donetsk, election officials travelled between settlements accompanied by police and armed military personnel. The footage does not show how many people had voted or provide any figures for turnout at the time it was filmed.

Ukraine's Security Service (SBU) has warned residents in occupied areas not to take part, saying that organising or promoting the elections could be a criminal offence under Ukrainian law, punishable by up to 10 years in prison. Yet the question remains: what choice do people have when armed soldiers are at their door?

Kyiv and Western governments consider elections held in occupied Ukrainian territory illegal, describing them as a "sham election" intended to legitimise Moscow's control over the regions.

articles.title: FBI Director Kash Patel clashes with Democrats at oversight hearing
articles.summary: Lawmakers pressed FBI Director Kash Patel during a contentious oversight hearing on Tuesday about his leadership of a bureau that has seen massive changes since the start of President Donald Trump’s second term.
articles.body: WASHINGTON — Lawmakers pressed FBI Director Kash Patel during a contentious oversight hearing on Tuesday about his leadership of a bureau that has seen massive changes since the start of President Donald Trump’s second term. Patel faced scrutiny from Democrats about changes to the FBI’s hiring process amid firings and departures from the bureau since Trump retook office in January 2025. He also faced questions about his use of government aircraft. As he lashed out at Democrats in the room, an FBI X account launched attacks on several members of the Senate Judiciary Committee. Following several heated exchanges with Senate Democrats, Patel told Sen. Chuck Grassley, R-Iowa, that he “would appreciate it if you concluded this hearing.” Sen. Dick Durbin, the Illinois Democrat who is not seeking re-election this year, noted this will likely be his last FBI oversight hearing until retirement and said he was “disappointed” the Senate Judiciary Committee “has stood by” since Trump retook office in January 2025. “I look forward to a day, hopefully in the very near future, when this committee will fulfill its duty to hold Director Patel accountable for his leadership,” Durbin said. Sen. Cory Booker, D-N.J., compared Patel to a “thug” and said he was using the FBI “to go after reporters” and stonewalling members of Congress who had questions about his oversight of the FBI. Democrats also questioned Patel over reports of an investigation into leaks that resulted in a story in The Atlantic focusing on concerns about his personal behavior. In April, Patel filed a $250 million lawsuit against the magazine over the story that made allegations about his drinking, with Patel’s team saying the FBI director “does not drink to excess.” Republican Senate Judiciary members largely praised the FBI director. They discussed with Patel how the FBI was handling what they claimed was “weaponization” of law enforcement during the prior administrations. Republicans have complained former special counsel Jack Smith obtained records of legislators’ phone calls and accused him of spying, though Smith had obtained records of legislators’ communications with members of the executive branch because they turned up during the investigation into Jan. 6 and Trump’s efforts to overturn the 2020 election. Patel’s FBI has overseen the firing of numerous FBI employees who were involved in prior investigations into Trump, including individuals involved in the 2022 search of Mar-a-Lago that has been a particular focus for Trump. Joe diGenova, the 81-year-old Trump loyalist who had been heading a “grand conspiracy” probe targeting former law enforcement officials involved in Trump investigations, told NBC News that Patel had been “absolutely superb in supporting our investigation.” DiGenova resigned last week after a conflict with Justice Department leadership about the direction of the investigation. If Democrats take control of the House or Senate, Patel’s FBI is expected to face increased scrutiny and investigations.

articles.title: Pentagon reveals secret space weapons are already in orbit — but won't say what they do
articles.summary: Air Force Secretary Troy Meink revealed the Space Force has on-orbit space control weapons, but the Pentagon won't say what they are or how they work.
articles.body: The U.S. has weapons orbiting Earth that can be used to defend American forces from attacks in space, the Air Force secretary revealed this week in a rare public acknowledgment of capabilities the Pentagon has largely kept secret. Air Force Secretary Troy Meink said Monday that the Space Force now has "on-orbit space control weapons capable of defending the joint force against hostile adversary action," but declined to say what the weapons are, how they work or when they were deployed. The carefully worded disclosure marks a shift in how openly the U.S. military talks about weapons in orbit as China and Russia develop their own capabilities to disrupt, disable or destroy satellites. TRUMP TO TRANSFORM SPACEFLIGHT FROM SPECTACLE TO STATUS QUO TARGETING 3 LAUNCHES PER DAY "Is there any question in the room, by anybody, about whether or not the Chinese or Russians have been developing these sorts of weapons?" Meink told reporters after his remarks at the Air & Space Forces Association’s Air, Space & Cyber Conference in National Harbor, Maryland — right outside of Washington, D.C. "For over a decade, we’ve been talking about the fact, and we have expressed concern, that the Chinese and Russians were developing weapons for space," he continued. "We need to focus on making sure we can protect ourselves operating in that environment." Exactly what the U.S. has put into orbit remains a mystery. The U.S. has previously discussed placing weapons in space, including plans to deploy space-based interceptors capable of destroying incoming missiles as part of President Donald Trump’s Golden Dome missile defense system. But Meink’s disclosure goes a step further: The Space Force already has weapons in orbit for "space control," a mission aimed at protecting U.S. access to space and, if necessary, denying an adversary the ability to use it. The Pentagon has historically revealed little about the weapons developed for that mission, with publicly known U.S. counter-space capabilities largely based on the ground. "What the U.S. is going for is a wow factor here," Clayton Swope, deputy director of the Aerospace Security Project at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, told Fox News Digital. "Wow. The U.S. has never talked about space weapons like this before." "That's really what is exceptional and newsworthy about this revelation," Swope said. "The U.S. is saying we're putting weapons in space to make sure that our adversaries can't use space, or to make sure that we can continue to use space." Meink appeared to make clear that the ambiguity surrounding the weapons is intentional. He told reporters his language was "very well thought out" and declined to say whether the systems are kinetic or non-kinetic. Kinetic weapons physically strike or destroy a target — think bombs, bullets and missile — while non-kinetic systems can disrupt or disable it without blowing it up — like cyber attacks or radio jams. "There are a lot of factors that roll into how we talk about these things," Meink said, explaining that publicly revealing a capability can contribute to deterrence while disclosing too much about it can undermine that advantage. "We’re not going to talk about the specifics of what we’re doing, whether we’ve tested it, not tested it, or anything else," he said. That leaves a wide range of possibilities. Fox News Digital did not hear back from the Space Force when reached for details of the weapon. INSIDE AMERICA'S LASER REVOLUTION AS THE MILITARY NEARS BIG BATTLEFIELD BREAKTHROUGH Swope said "space control weapons" could encompass everything from kinetic systems capable of firing missiles or projectiles at another satellite to jammers that interfere with satellite communications or lasers designed to temporarily overwhelm imaging sensors. "We really don't have enough information to know precisely which one of these types of capabilities we're talking about," Swope said. "It's really anybody's guess what type of weapon we're talking about." FATAL AIR AMBULANCE CRASH EXPOSES GROWING GPS DANGER FACING US FLIGHTS But whatever the Pentagon has deployed, putting a weapon in orbit rather than launching it from Earth could offer one potentially significant advantage: speed and surprise. A weapon launched from Earth toward a satellite could potentially give an adversary warning that an attack was underway. A capability already positioned in orbit could dramatically shorten that window. "Maybe something measured at dozens of minutes could be compressed into just mere minutes," Swope said. "And you wouldn't have any indication that maybe a jammer was turned on, on the satellite, other than all of a sudden your signal is being interfered with," he added. "If you can act fast without your adversary knowing, if you can have surprise, that gives you a strategic or an asymmetric advantage in combat," Swope said. "And having systems in orbit do just that." Even observing the spacecraft itself may offer few clues about what it can do. "Space is a very transparent place," Swope said, noting that governments and civilian observers can track where satellites are, how fast they are moving and what orbits they occupy. "But what you'll see often is, oh, it's a satellite," he said. "It's a lot of technology with solar panels and antenna on it. And you don't really know much beyond that." A satellite equipped to jam another spacecraft’s signals, for example, might look much like an ordinary communications satellite. "Any signal can be a jamming signal," Swope said. "It just depends on if it's the one you want to receive, or the one that someone's trying to use to jam you." The concept of weapons operating in orbit is not new. Swope pointed to the Soviet Union’s work on co-orbital anti-satellite weapons dating to the 1960s. Russia has continued developing counterspace capabilities, including systems designed to operate in orbit near other satellites. China has also developed and tested technologies that could threaten spacecraft, including satellite-servicing and debris-removal systems that have legitimate civilian uses but could potentially be repurposed to interfere with another satellite. Other forms of interference are already widespread. "When we talk about jamming and spoofing and cyberattacks against space systems, these happen all the time, both from Russia and China and other countries like North Korea and Iran," Swope said. "There is so much jamming and spoofing happening around the world right now, it's almost ubiquitous." Those attacks can target systems such as GPS and satellite communications without physically destroying a spacecraft. That distinction could become critical during a conflict. Jamming, spoofing or cyberattacks may remain below the threshold that prompts a major military response, while physically destroying a satellite could represent a significant escalation. "If you drop a bomb on a satellite ground station or you shoot a missile at a satellite in space, that's a big difference," Swope said. "That's a huge escalation." The stakes are particularly high because modern U.S. warfare is deeply dependent on space-based systems for communications, navigation, intelligence, missile warning and targeting. "Space is an enabler of joint operations," Swope said. "We can't do military operations the way that we do them today without satellites, without systems in space." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP China increasingly faces the same dependency, making control of space potentially decisive in a conflict between the two powers. "Whoever has space and can deny that to their adversary has a huge asymmetric advantage in a conflict," Swope said. "China depends on space as well, and their use of space for joint operations looks very much like the United States," he added. "Both countries, I would go so far as to say, depend on space to conduct military operations on Earth."

articles.title: Two Democrats cross aisle to help tee up final vote on Russia sanctions bill
articles.summary: The House advanced legislation on Tuesday that grants President Trump tariff authorities on countries purchasing Russian energy and extends existing sanctions on Iran, clearing a major procedural hurdle for the Russia Sanctions Act.
articles.body:
The House on Tuesday advanced legislation that would grant President Trump tariff authorities on countries who purchase Russian energy and extend existing sanctions on Iran, clearing a major procedural hurdle.

The rule, teeing up a final vote on the legislation, appeared headed for defeat until two Democrats — for the second time in as many weeks — broke precedent and voted to advance the measure. Reps. Jared Golden (Maine) and Marie Gluesenkamp Perez (Wash.) also broke with Democrats on a rule vote earlier this month, shocking House Democratic leaders . Rule votes are typically seen as a test of party loyalty, and it is unusual for Democrats to cross the aisle in support of them.

Their votes brought the tally to 214-211 on the rule that included the Russia sanctions bill —championed by the late Sen. Lindsey Graham (R-S.C.) — teeing up a debate and final vote on the legislation.

The rule vote served as a victory for the bill’s backers, like Rep. Michael McCaul (R-Texas), who overcame pushback from both inside the GOP and from Democrats. Before Tuesday’s vote, the resistance left some predicting the bill was “dead again” following nearly a year and a half of negotiations.

Rep. Tim Burchett (R-Tenn.), who voted with Democrats against the bill, told The Hill he got an agreement with GOP leaders to take action on the issue of fuel cost reduction.

“I just want to make sure America gets some reduction in fuel costs, and the greedy fuel companies are sticking it to us, and we don’t have the guts to do anything about it,” he said. He added that GOP leaders promised they would get a measure on the floor to deal with the matter. “They’re going to do something. Let us vote on something that would hopefully reduce the price of fuel, but we’ll see,” Burchett said.

In remarks during a Monday House Rules Committee hearing, McCaul framed Tuesday’s vote on the Russia sanctions bill as critical in sending a message to Russian President Vladimir Putin about U.S. support for Ukraine and warning Chinese President Xi Jinping against attempting aggression against Taiwan.

“Senator Lindsey Graham understood these global threats well, and that’s why he spent more than a year working on this legislation, which I promised him I would introduce in the House,” the Texas representative said.

He continued, “Lindsey Graham was my friend. He was my mentor. He understood the threats facing this country and had the courage to stand up and confront the.”

“We shared a fundamental belief that America is strongest at home when it projects strength abroad …This is a moral issue that requires moral courage. When we look back on this moment, I want us to be able to say that we did everything possible to end this war,” McCaul concluded.

Democratic opponents, despite their support for Ukraine, argued the bill granted Trump tariff authorities the Supreme Court had already shut down.

Democratic Reps. Don Beyer (Va.), a senior House Democrat of Congress’s Joint Economic Committee; Gregory Meeks (N.Y.), the ranking member of the House Foreign Affairs Committee; and Richard Neal (Mass.), the ranking member of the House Ways and Means Committee, argued in a joint statement last week that the bill would do “more harm than good.”

“This bill would dramatically expand presidential tariff authorities while failing to mandate sanctions on Russia, both of which are unacceptable. These flaws would raise Americans’ prices while undermining support for Ukraine in the long term. We continue to seek bicameral, bipartisan negotiations to craft a bill that can win strong support in both chambers and deliver on our promise to Ukraine,” they wrote.

But even some of Trump’s most outspoken critics, who are opposed to giving the president tariff authorities, said defeating the bill would actually harm U.S. support for Ukraine and embolden Putin.

“The positive symbolism of it passing outweighs the negative symbolism of it failing. If it fails, Putin will cheer & Ukrainians will be disappointed,” Michael McFaul, who served as U.S. ambassador to Russia during the Obama administration, posted on social platform X .

“I also have no illusions that Trump will actually use the authorities in the legislature to impose ‘crippling’ sanctions on Russia. He won’t,” he added.

The vote on the bill is taking place during the “Ukraine Action Summit,” a major lobbying initiative over the course of the week, bringing more than 600 constituencies from 50 states and Puerto Rico advocating for Congress to pass the Russia Sanctions Act.

“The Sanctioning Russia Act is the number one priority for Ukraine advocacy right now,” summit organizer Eugene Goncharov, the American Coalition for Ukraine’s policy director, said.

Goncharov voiced support for the latest version of the bill, saying it expands the list of sanctions on Russian military figures and foreign suppliers, bans new U.S. investment in Russia, targets Russia’s shadow fleet of oil tankers — used to evade sanctions — and tightens restrictions on exports to Russia that could be used by its military.

The bill further includes sanctions authority for those responsible for the abduction of Ukrainian children and extends sanctions on Iran.

“This is the bill that is likely to pass and be signed into law, and when that happens, it will make this war harder and more expensive for Russia to keep fighting,” Goncharov said.

articles.title: Finneas withdraws from Ed Sheeran tour over Macklemore ouster
articles.summary: Billie Eilish’s brother and music collaborator Finneas is the latest of several artists that have pulled out of Ed Sheeran’s tour after rapper Macklemore was removed for delivering a “free Palestine” message. Finneas joins Danish band Lukas Graham, Irish band Beoga and Aaron Rowe in announcing that they would no longer open for Sheeran on…
articles.body:
Billie Eilish’s brother and music collaborator Finneas is the latest of several artists that have pulled out of Ed Sheeran’s tour after rapper Macklemore was removed for delivering a “free Palestine” message.

Finneas joins Danish band Lukas Graham, Irish band Beoga and Aaron Rowe in announcing that they would no longer open for Sheeran on his Loop tour. Their exits, which Sheeran said were not his decision, leave the tour without any supporting acts.

“Artists must not be silenced when they speak up for the oppressed,” Finneas wrote on social media . “I have decided to withdraw from my upcoming tour dates with Ed Sheeran. I stand with Palestine and its people.”

Finneas was scheduled to open six shows in South America later this year.

Pro-Israel groups went after Macklemore after he delivered a pro-Palestine message in an opening set for Sheeran at Metlife Stadium last month, according to the Hollywood Reporter .

In a Monday post on social media, Macklemore said Sheeran told him that Robert Kraft, who owns the Gillette Stadium where they were scheduled to perform later this month, called him asking to remove Macklemore from the set.

“Ed told me that Kraft said I would not be allowed to perform in his stadium. Ed also told me that Kraft had rallied some of the other stadium owners and collectively they gave him an ultimatum: if Macklemore stays on the tour, you will not be allowed to play in our venues,” the Seattle rapper said.

Macklemore stood by his pro-Palestine stance, adding that if “turning the conversation back to Palestine” was the reason for his ouster, “it was the most successful tour I’ve ever been on.”

Lukas Graham attributed its exit from the show to the ongoing war in Gaza and the deaths of civilians.

“We should be able to speak about war, about civilians being killed, about children who deserve to group up,” the band said. “Wherever they live. Whatever flag flies over them.”

Rowe and Beoga announced similar decisions Tuesday, saying they were leaving in support of Macklemore and Palestinians.

articles.title: Trump: Kennedy Center won’t be renovated if courts deny board’s naming plan
articles.summary: President Trump said Tuesday that the Kennedy Center will not be renovated if courts shoot down the naming plan chosen by the center’s board. “The Board of The Kennedy Center today agreed, almost unanimously, to close the Building for Safety reasons, and so that it can begin the process of Reconstruction,” the president said in…
articles.body:
President Trump said Tuesday that the Kennedy Center will not be renovated if courts shoot down the naming plan chosen by the center’s board.

“The Board of The Kennedy Center today agreed, almost unanimously, to close the Building for Safety reasons, and so that it can begin the process of Reconstruction,” the president said in a post on his Truth Social platform Tuesday afternoon. “The closing will take place immediately, however, the Renovation and Reconstruction, which is a very large and complex job, cannot begin until such time as the D.C. Circuit rules on the Board’s approved name.”

“If the ruling is a negative one, which it should not be, and is not overturned by the U.S. Supreme Court, the Reconstruction and the Renovation of The Kennedy Center will not take place,” the president added.

On Tuesday, a federal judge blocked an effort by the Kennedy Center to inscribe Trump’s name on the building, as well as rename the campus after the president.

U.S. District Judge Christopher Cooper ruled that the Kennedy Center board, handpicked by the president, could not go ahead with plans without approval from Congress and found that a vote on the renaming last month probably violated his prior injunction.

“The board resolution bucks a federal court order and a statute Congress enacted,” Cooper, an Obama appointee, said in his opinion.

The board voted also voted Tuesday to immediately close the institution’s main building for renovations, a source familiar with the situation told The Hill. The board has asserted that only the president can raise enough money to save the Kennedy Center.

The board’s vote followed officials signaling the performing arts center was dealing with “certain fiscal collapse within weeks.” A draft resolution labeled the Kennedy Center as close to bankruptcy.

articles.body:
The House Oversight Committee on Tuesday in a unanimous bipartisan vote held Leon Black in contempt of Congress after he failed to appear for the deposition related to his ties to deceased sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

Lawmakers have sought to question Black, who co-founded Apollo Global Management, about payments he made to Epstein totaling millions over a number of years. The investor says the payments were for tax and estate planning, among other services, and he had no knowledge of any abuse.

Black walked out of a voluntary interview with the panel two months ago, and he sued the committee earlier this month on the day he was commanded to appear for a deposition.

“Mr. Black is hiding behind litigation to delay having to provide answers to the American people. No one is above the law. Mr. Black will be treated the same as anyone else in this investigation, and his actions have consequences. A little over two months ago, Mr. Black appeared before the committee for a transcribed interview, but only an hour into the interview, he began refusing to answer questions,” Chair James Comer (R-Ky.) said at the start of the hearing.

“Subpoenas are not suggestions; they carry the force of law and require full compliance.”

Comer said in addition to failing to comply with the subpoena for a deposition, Black also only supplied one nondisclosure agreement following a subpoena for documents, despite an indication from his attorneys that there were additional documents.

Ranking member Robert Garcia (D-Calif.) said the panel had numerous questions about Black’s financial ties to Epstein.

“We believe that Leon Black is at the heart of the Epstein network. This is a private equity billionaire worth roughly $13 billion dollars. We need to know why Jeffrey Epstein got over 180 million dollars from Mr. Black. We know this money enabled Epstein’s activities for years, and we need to know how and if it led to the abuse of women and girls. We need to know about Leon Black and Jeffrey Epstein’s financial dealings,” he said during the business meeting.

Black’s legal team did not immediately respond to request for comment.

His lawsuit, however, argues the committee lacks legal authority to enforce the subpoenas and that they improperly seek private information.

“Additionally, the subpoenas would also expose women who value their privacy, who have no known or public connection to Epstein, who bargained for confidentiality and have refused to release it, and who have no ability to protect themselves and their privacy before the Committee,” the complaint states.

A contempt resolution must be brought to the full House floor for consideration. If it is approved, it acts as a referral to the Justice Department, which must then determine whether to press charges.

The vote was the latest example of bipartisanship when it comes to investigating the dealings of Jeffrey Epstein.

The House voted earlier this year to force the Justice Department to release files related to the deceased financier while the committee has requested to speak with or compelled interviews from numerous subjects.

In July, Comer said he would also like to hear from Attorney General Todd Blanche.

articles.title: Comey asks to push trial in seashell case to February
articles.summary: Former FBI Director James Comey on Tuesday asked that his trial on charges of threatening President Trump’s life with seashells styled to spell “86 47” be moved to February. Comey had previously motioned to have the trial start Oct. 21. His latest motion, written by defense attorney Joseph Zeszotarski Jr., requested that the date be…
articles.body:
Former FBI Director James Comey on Tuesday asked that his trial on charges of threatening President Trump’s life with seashells styled to spell “86 47” be moved to February.

Comey had previously motioned to have the trial start Oct. 21 . His latest motion, written by defense attorney Joseph Zeszotarski Jr., requested that the date be moved “because additional time is needed to prepare for trial,” according to court documents.

Zeszotarski added that this includes time to prepare for any pretrial hearings, review discovery material and to consider and draft “various motions in limine.”

The Department of Justice (DOJ) secured a second indictment against Comey in April in connection with a since-deleted Instagram post featuring the seashells in the sands of a North Carolina beach. The indictment claimed that the photo was a “serious expression of an intent to do harm” to Trump.

Comey has denied all wrongdoing, with his defense team previously arguing that “’86’ simply means ‘get rid of’ or ‘eject’ and has no violent connotation except in the most uncommon usages.”

Restaurant employees frequently use the term “86” when an item is unavailable or needs to be removed. The Merriam-Webster dictionary states that “86” originated from 1930s soda-counter slang indicating that an item was sold out.

The former FBI director’s legal team said in his motion to toss the case in July that their client was being targeted for exercising his First Amendment right by “publishing another person’s statement of political opposition.” They also argued that there is no definition of “86,” as seen in a dictionary, meaning “to kill.”

The DOJ discouraged the judge from tossing the case, stating that the photo of the seashells constituted a “true threat” to the president. Prosecutors argued that Comey acknowledged that some may have construed his post as a threat when he deleted it.

Comey wrote that he deleted the post after he “assumed” the shells were arranged in a “political message” and that he did not “realize some folks associate those numbers with violence,” leading him to delete the post, according to a May 2025 Instagram post .

Trump accused Comey of knowing what the message intended, telling Fox News’s Bret Baier in May 2025 that it “meant assassination.”

Comey is a longtime foe of the president and has publicly criticized Trump in the past. The president fired him FBI director in 2017 and the former FBI head later backed former Vice President Kamala Harris’s presidential bid in 2024 and former President Biden’s bid in 2020.

articles.title: The Memo: Blanche blasts through norms as Rose Garden ‘press secretary’
articles.summary: An administration that often exhibits ostentatious pride in bursting through norms did so yet again Tuesday afternoon, when Attorney General Todd Blanche took a turn as de facto White House press secretary. Blanche spoke to reporters in the Rose Garden, mixing together commentary on legal matters, praise of Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s prosecution of the…
articles.body:
An administration that often exhibits ostentatious pride in bursting through norms did so yet again Tuesday afternoon, when Attorney General Todd Blanche took a turn as de facto White House press secretary.

Blanche spoke to reporters in the Rose Garden, mixing together commentary on legal matters, praise of Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s prosecution of the Iran war, jabs at the Biden administration, an insistence the United States had to win the AI race and even some careful comments about the recent wedding of Donald Trump Jr.

Blanche also took the time to poke fun at the assembled media — albeit with a demeanor that did not suggest any great mirth on his part.

“I notice you guys are sweating, which is nice. I love to see that,” he said just before taking questions.

“I’m very sorry that you’re sweating. I’m not really sorry,” he said near the end.

The mere fact that Blanche, a former personal lawyer to Trump, now serves as attorney general is exceptional in itself. The attorney general and the Department of Justice (DOJ) have traditionally been seen as without precise parallels elsewhere in government.

The DOJ and its leader have been expected to demonstrate some level of independence from the political wishes of the president they serve. Equally, past presidents have — for the most part — sought to avoid the appearance that they are pushing the DOJ in ways that would erode this perception.

The extent to which such niceties have been truly observed is debatable, to be sure. But it is hard to imagine a banner with the president’s face being unfurled from the DOJ’s Washington headquarters previously, as has been the case during this administration.

Trump, for his part, famously and publicly appealed to Blanche’s predecessor, Pam Bondi, to speed up prosecution of his enemies. He has at various times named other foes he believes should be targeted, only for prosecutors to follow through.

This has led to some embarrassing outcomes — such as when a grand jury declined in February to return indictments against six Democratic lawmakers who had released a video urging U.S. troops not to obey illegal orders.

Trump suggested their actions amounted to “seditious behavior.” The grand jurors didn’t even accept there was a case to answer.

Blanche’s appearance wasn’t even the first transgressive act of the day from within the administration.

FBI Director Kash Patel earlier was asked by lawmakers about the lifting of the bureau’s previous automatic ban on new trainees if they had been found to engage in prostitution or bestiality.

Less luridly, but more controversially, Trump had inveighed against the Supreme Court on social media earlier Tuesday. His anger had been sparked by an adverse ruling the previous evening, in which the high court rejected Trump’s bid to restrict mail-in voting in time for the midterm elections.

Trump’s reaction was to complain that “The Supreme Court has really let our Country down!” and to further insist, “Certain Justices are petrified of these crazed and depraved Democrats, and are totally unable to show the courage necessary to save our America.”

Trump also asserted, in jeering reference to the three justices he nominated during his first term: “These are not the people I interviewed to serve on the United States Supreme Court, they are merely a shell of their original selves.”

The court ruling came in sparse form Monday evening, but Team Trump appeared to have lost 7-2, with none of his three nominees — Justices Neil Gorsuch, Brett Kavanaugh and Amy Coney Barrett — fully backing him.

Blanche, in the Rose Garden, cast the media storm that immediately followed Trump’s comments as much ado about nothing. He said the administration would “of course” follow the ruling but also continue its efforts to ensure a “fair election.”

“He is very frustrated,” the attorney general said of the president. “He has every right — and indeed he should — communicate his concerns with the Supreme Court whenever he has them.”

Later, Blanche was asked whether, during his time in private practice, he would have advised a client to take on a court in the manner of Trump’s blasts at the Supreme Court. The attorney general rejected the comparison.

“He’s the president of the United States, so the real question is whether the president of the United States is allowed to be critical of another branch of government,” Blanche said. “And the answer to that is: Absolutely, of course he is.”

At times, the attorney general was more circumspect. He largely evaded a question about whether he asked for the resignation of Joe DiGenova, a fervently pro-Trump figure and former U.S. attorney for the District of Columbia who had been investigating whether there was a “conspiracy” against Trump during previous Democratic administrations.

A separate question about a seeming lack of action following the FBI’s controversial raid on a Fulton County, Ga., election hub in January also elicited little real information.

Still, he was not always so cautious. He alleged that, in a previous incarnation, the FBI had sought to put Trump “in prison till he dies.”

Pressed on questions around the ethics of a Russian oligarch paying for some of the wedding celebrations for Donald Trump Jr. and his new wife, Bettina, in May, Blanche shot back to a reporter: “When you say, ‘Am I investigating,’ am I investigating what? And when you say this person is a friend of Putin, I don’t even know if that’s true or not.”

The person in question, Umar Kremlev, had been bestowed a state honor by Putin, according to investigative website ProPublica, which broke the story.

Elsewhere, the nation’s chief law enforcement officer provided praise for Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth, who he said was doing a “phenomenal job”; and for former White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt, who Blanche praised for her handling of the job he was trying to fill, at least for about 35 minutes.

“She’s a lot better than me,” the attorney general said.

The Memo is a reported column by Niall Stanage.

articles.title: GOP shifts message on costs as Iran war drags on: From the Politics Desk
articles.summary: In today’s edition, Sahil Kapur examines how the Iran war is undercutting what was once a political advantage for Republicans.
articles.body: Welcome to From the Politics Desk, a daily newsletter that brings you the NBC News Politics team’s latest reporting and analysis from the White House, Capitol Hill and the campaign trail. In today’s edition, Sahil Kapur examines how the Iran war is undercutting what was once a political advantage for Republicans. Plus, Lawrence Hurley takes stock of two big election-related rulings from the Supreme Court. — Adam Wollner GOP shifts message on costs with Iran war expected to drag beyond midterms Analysis by Sahil Kapur House Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., made a candid admission today that President Donald Trump’s war against Iran — and the resulting chaos in the Strait of Hormuz — has driven up prices for Americans. Echoing comments Trump made last week, Johnson said the situation won’t be resolved until after the midterm elections. “Look, we’re going to acknowledge, obviously, gas prices are too high right now, diesel prices are too high. There’s a very simple reason for it. It’s tied, of course, to the Strait of Hormuz. We have got to get commerce stabilized in the Strait of Hormuz,” Johnson told reporters after a GOP meeting. “Gas prices will immediately come down again. The cost of groceries will, as well, because that’s tied in many ways to the cost of transport, of getting the goods to the market.” “And so that Iranian situation, the Strait of Hormuz — as soon as that’s resolved, it comes down. Now, the president has forecast, you’ve heard him even in recent days, he thinks it can get done maybe right after the election,” he said. Johnson’s remarks make it clear that Republicans have lost hope that the Iran war will end before the midterms and have accepted that there’s no way around the economic fallout other than to address it directly. It’s a messaging shift after numerous GOP strategists had hoped the war would end in time for Americans to see some reduction in costs before they head to the polls. And a new survey highlights the economic headwinds facing Republicans. A New York Times/Siena University poll found that 38% of likely voters approved of Trump’s job performance. On the economy, voters’ No. 1 issue, his approval rating was 39%, and on the cost of living, it sank to 28%. As for the Iran war, 31% approved of Trump’s handling of it. It culminated in a startling finding: Likely voters now trust Democrats over Republicans on the economy (by 7 points), the cost of living (by 8 points) and even the deficit (by 10 points). The poll also found Democrats leading by nearly 9 points on the generic congressional ballot. Democrats hope to take full advantage, with House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., labeling the Iran conflict “a reckless and costly war of choice” by Trump that has harmed Americans. Republicans have long enjoyed voter trust on those issues. The economy was an asset for Trump not just in 2024 (when his party scored big wins), but also in 2020 (which helped the GOP overperform downballot and keep Democratic margins to a minimum) and in 2016 (which fueled Trump’s upset win over Hillary Clinton). In the 2024 election, exit polls found that the economy ranked as the top issue for voters, and those who prioritized it preferred Trump over Kamala Harris by 81% to 18%. Voters said they trusted Trump over Harris to handle the economy by 53% to 46%. Johnson insisted that the previous administration was the root of Americans’ economic woes. “We’re not there yet. It takes a long time to turn the aircraft carrier, the ship of state. We’re pulling out of the most disastrous situation that we inherited after Biden-Harris.” Kyle Stewart contributed. More on the economy: 📈 Inflation watch: A new report released by the Congressional Budget Office found the Iran war was responsible for more than one-third of the increase in inflation this year.💲 Bond watch: The yield on the 10-year Treasury note hit 5.04% earlier today, the highest since 2007. More on the midterms: 🗺️ House landscape: The number of true battleground districts is smaller than in past elections, Ben Kamisar writes. Just 15 districts account for more than half of the $575 million already spent and reserved for advertising in House races from Labor Day to Election Day.🗳️ Data Dive: In the latest edition of his newsletter, Steve Kornacki digs into the shifts among two key voting groups that help explain Democrat James Talarico’s strength in the polls in the Texas Senate race. Supreme Court pushes back against Trump and the GOP’s election plans By Lawrence Hurley The Supreme Court in the last week has delivered major blows to President Donald Trump and his fellow Republicans that suggest the justices will not be receptive to last-minute efforts to change election rules heading into the midterms. Last night, the court blocked Trump’s plan to exert federal control over mail-in ballots via a Postal Service regulation. The decision came after the court twice last week ruled against Republicans by declining to revive a new congressional map in Missouri that would have eliminated one of two Democratic-held districts. While the court has a 6-3 conservative majority that often rules for Republican priorities, there are limits to how receptive some justices are to more extreme requests, election law experts told NBC News. That’s especially true for cases that could disrupt voters when an election is close or already underway. “I think the court is going to pay very close attention to any extraordinary actions that destabilize the electoral process,” said Bob Bauer, who was White House counsel for President Barack Obama. “There’s a signal here that this sort of late intervention is going to receive scrutiny.” Trump’s response: “It is a big loss for Republicans, and America itself, and makes cheating by the Radical Left ‘Dumocrats,’ on Mail-In Ballots, a much easier thing to do — And now they have an open field to do so!” Trump said on Truth Social, repeating his unfounded claims about widespread election fraud. Trump called the two dissenting justices, Samuel Alito and Clarence Thomas, “legends” and criticized the three justices he appointed to the court. “These are not the people I interviewed to serve on the United States Supreme Court, they are merely a shell of their original selves,” Trump said. Read more → That’s all From the Politics Desk for now. Today’s newsletter was compiled by Adam Wollner. If you have feedback — likes or dislikes — email us at politicsnewsletter@nbcuni.com And if you’re a fan, please share with everyone and anyone. They can sign up here.

articles.title: High-profile Democrat breaks with party, embraces key pieces of Trump agenda
articles.summary: Haley Stevens backs Trump administration policies on critical minerals, data centers and public equity stakes in high-growth industries like Intel.
articles.body: DETROIT, MICHIGAN — Rep. Haley Stevens, D-Mich., threw her support behind three of the Trump administration’s signature economic policies in an interview with Fox News Digital. Collaboration between ratepayers and data center developers, public stakes in high-growth industries and loan guarantees for critical mineral extraction are all areas where the Michigan congresswoman says the Trump administration is charting the right course. She also pointed to bolstering American manufacturing and deterring the nation’s adversaries from hostage taking as areas where she believes bipartisan collaboration is possible. "It's not just about taxation," Stevens told Fox News Digital when asked how revenues can be raised to fund healthcare and infrastructure programs. "If federal dollars are used, like what Mr. Elon Musk got from the federal government, so potentially this current administration could be right that ownership stakes should be on the table." PROGRESSIVE PRAISE FOR TRUMP AS WARREN BACKS PUSH TO CURB DEFENSE CONTRACTOR CEO PAYOUTS The Trump administration has increasingly pursued direct equity stakes, alongside grants and loans, to steer capital into industries it considers strategically important, such as semiconductors and critical minerals. For instance, the administration converted $8.9 billion in federal funding into a 9.9% nonvoting stake in Intel, while the Pentagon took a 15% stake in rare-earth producer MP Materials. Both investments have increased in value since the government took them, although those gains are not realized until the shares are sold. While Stevens thinks stimulating economic growth is part of the equation for balancing the federal balance sheet, she did say that the "wealthiest of the wealthy" should "absolutely" pay more in taxes. Stevens rose to national prominence during her primary contest against Abdul El-Sayed, who has since become the Democratic nominee for Senate in Michigan. She cast herself as a more moderate alternative to El-Sayed, who she accused of unfairly singling out Jewish Americans. DEMOCRATS' CIVIL WAR HEADS TO MICHIGAN WHERE PROGRESSIVES FACE BIGGEST TEST YET IN HIGH-STAKES SENATE SHOWDOWN Though the primary feud between the two was intense, Stevens endorsed El-Sayed following a narrow primary defeat and signaled that, while she may agree with President Donald Trump on some things, she still sees his broader agenda as dangerous for America. "I personally think [Republican nominee] Mike Rogers is going to continue to rubber-stamp Donald Trump’s chaotic agenda," she said in an interview after endorsing El-Sayed. "People are going to make a personal and private decision. I am not on the ballot in Michigan." Likewise, the White House isn't particularly warm towards Stevens. "It’s rich that Haley Stevens claims to support President Trump’s proven economic agenda after voting against the President over 80 percent of the time in Congress – including on the Great One Big Beautiful Bill, which is the largest working-class tax cut in history," White House spokesman Kush Desai told Fox News Digital. MICHIGAN DEMOCRAT HALEY STEVENS BACKS EL-SAYED AFTER NARROW PRIMARY DEFEAT, CALLS SOCIALISM ‘DANGEROUS’ Though Stevens is a loyal Democrat, she says that doesn’t prevent her from working across the aisle, especially on local issues. For that reason, she threw her support behind the Trump administration’s Ratepayer Protection Pledge, a collaborative framework bringing together utilities, data center developers, cooperatives and state governments to keep energy prices down amidst the massive buildout of AI infrastructure. "I think collaboration is always a promising first step and path forward," Stevens told Fox News Digital when asked about the Ratepayer Protection Pledge. "Before I was in Congress, I had also worked on the bipartisan auto-rescue task force in the Obama administration. I was an Obama appointee, but there were also Bush appointees who stayed on, and there frankly were Republicans who were on the task force. And the reason I'm mentioning the auto task force is that we coordinated at the local level. We coordinated large-scale federal resources." Later in the interview, Stevens stressed to Fox News Digital that she is "really fired up about critical minerals," arguing that America makes itself vulnerable to China by failing to increase domestic production. She listed loan guarantees for mining firms, a policy currently being carried out by the Trump administration, as something she supports. WEST VIRGINIA UNIVERSITY RESEARCHERS TURN POLLUTED MINE WATER INTO CRITICAL RARE EARTH MINERALS The White House did not respond to a request for comment when reached by Fox News Digital on Tuesday. Looking forward, Stevens — who has a strong record of bipartisan work — highlighted a few areas she believes are fertile ground for Republicans and Democrats to work together. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "[Rep.] French Hill, who's a Republican from Arkansas and a great congressman, French Hill and I have passed considerable pieces of legislation to stand up to America's enemies, to stand up to our detractors, and that continues to be an area where I believe that we will see more bipartisan collaboration," she told Fox News Digital. "I also feel very strongly and I'm very proud to serve as the bipartisan caucus chair of the manufacturing caucus, our industrial sector, and one of the areas of great success for me in the Congress was, as a midwesterner, working with colleagues on the other side of the aisle to grow our manufacturing economy."

articles.title: Wicker, Shaheen to propose resolution urging U.S. cooperation with Russian pro-democracy movement
articles.summary: A pair of influential bipartisan Senators plan to introduce a resolution Wednesday calling on the State Department to bolster cooperation with Russia’s pro-democracy movement inside and outside the country, according to a draft obtained exclusively by The Hill. Sens. Roger Wicker (R-Miss.) and Jeanne Shaheen (D-N.H.) introduced the non-binding resolution to coincide with a major…
articles.body:
A pair of influential bipartisan Senators plan to introduce a resolution Wednesday calling on the State Department to bolster cooperation with Russia’s pro-democracy movement inside and outside the country, according to a draft obtained exclusively by The Hill.

Sens. Roger Wicker (R-Miss.) and Jeanne Shaheen (D-N.H.) introduced the non-binding resolution to coincide with a major gathering of Russian dissidents in Washington D.C., called the Washington Dialogue.

It’s the second time the dialogue has convened, sponsored by the National Endowment for Democracy, the Congressionally-funded democracy promotion organization, and the Free Russia Foundation, founded by Russian dissidents, including those who have served time in Putin’s jails and been freed with U.S. intervention.

The resolution condemns Russian President Vladimir Putin’s repression at home and the war against Ukraine, along with Russia’s detention of Americans, including Stephen Hubbard . He was captured by Russian forces after the invasion of Ukraine, accused of fighting as a mercenary for Ukraine. Hubbard denies he is a soldier and he is designated by the U.S. as wrongfully detained.

Wicker, the chairman of the Senate Armed Services Committee, said the resolution honored assassinated Russian political activists — specifically Boris Nemtsov, a prominent Putin critic who was killed in 2015 by gunmen with alleged links to the Russian government ; and the prominent Putin opponent, Alexei Navalny. European governments blamed the Russian government for Navalny’s death by poison in 2024.

“My colleague Senator Shaheen and I introduce this resolution for Nemtsov, for Navalny, and for the courageous Russians who carry their torch today,” Wicker said in a statement provided to The Hill.

“Putin casts a repressive shadow over Russia, but these heroes work toward a bright future they cannot yet see. The U.S. Senate honors their efforts and looks forward to the day when Russia is led by and for its people.”

Shaheen, in a statement to The Hill, said the resolution aims to “champion those who fight for democracy within Russia and hold the Russian government accountable for the crimes it has committed against its own people.”

“Putin’s war of aggression against Ukraine was rooted in his fear that the Russian people would see Ukraine’s progress in creating a more democratic, prosperous country and want the same for their own country,” said Shaheen, the ranking member of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee.

“Putin has used cruel tactics on his own people: suppressing dissent through brutal violence, proliferating state-sponsored repression and undermining democracy with election interference and through disinformation campaigns.”

The resolution acknowledges that it is in the national interest of the U.S. to support democratic actors in Russia, commends the work of Russian civil society and independent media to expose and respond to crimes by Putin’s government and pursue accountability.

The resolution comes ahead of Russian parliamentary elections taking place between September 18 and 20, the first to be held since Russia launched its full-scale invasion against Ukraine in Feb. 2022.

Putin’s party, United Russia, is widely expected to sweep the election, although close attention will be paid to whether the party can get the more than 300 seats needed for a super-majority and push through constitutional changes without other parties’ support.

Russia’s Supreme Court has barred the liberal Yabloko party from the party-list ballot, the only registered party to oppose Russia’s war in Ukraine, while other opposition politicians have been banned from running, Reuters reported .

Putin, in power as president or prime minister since 2000, has consolidated his control over the country by cracking down on any political opposition and imposing strict censorship to stifle independent media, connections to international organizations or free access to the internet.

There are an estimated 1,700 political prisoners in Russian jails, according to human rights monitors, and nearly one million Russians have left the country since Feb. 2022.

articles.title: EXCLUSIVE: Haitian illegal alien gang member who went viral yelling ‘Biden forever’ during ICE arrest deported
articles.summary: A Haitian gang member who shouted "Biden forever" during his viral ICE arrest has been deported to Haiti after spending 19 months in custody.
articles.body: EXCLUSIVE: A Haitian gang member and illegal alien who defiantly told Fox News cameras "I’m not going back to Haiti" and shouted "Biden forever" during his viral U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) arrest has been deported to Haiti by the Trump administration after spending 19 months in federal custody. Wisteguens Jean Quely Charles was deported on an ICE flight originating in Louisiana, the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) confirmed to Fox News. Sources told Fox News that Charles was extremely combative aboard the aircraft and made crude, profane and threatening remarks about President Donald Trump and his family during the deportation flight. DHS CHIEF MULLIN CLASHES WITH TAPPER OVER HAITI DEPORTATIONS AFTER SUPREME COURT TPS RULING An image obtained exclusively by Fox News shows Charles aboard the plane. The photo was provided by an ICE source and was not included among the images officially released by DHS. The deportation completes a dramatic reversal from Charles' arrest in Massachusetts on Jan. 22, 2025, when Fox News cameras captured him insisting he would not be returned to Haiti. "I’m not going back to Haiti … you feel me?" Charles said during the arrest. "F--- Trump," he added. "Biden forever bro." Fox News witnessed the arrest as ICE Enforcement and Removal Operations officers took Charles into custody in Massachusetts, just days after Trump returned to the White House. EXCLUSIVE: ICE NABS MULTIPLE CONVICTED KILLERS IN SINGLE DAY AMID NATIONWIDE IMMIGRATION SWEEP DHS identifies Charles as a member of the Back Block Money Gang and says he had accumulated 17 criminal convictions. His criminal history included convictions for assault and battery on a public employee, resisting arrest, assault and battery with a dangerous weapon, possession with intent to distribute a Class D controlled substance, possession of controlled substances, carrying a dangerous weapon, carrying ammunition without a firearm identification card and trespassing, according to DHS. Charles remained in federal custody for approximately 19 months after his arrest as his immigration case proceeded. A Department of Justice (DOJ) immigration judge issued Charles a final order of removal on Nov. 7, 2025, according to DHS. ICE MAKES NATIONWIDE ARRESTS OF ILLEGAL IMMIGRANTS, MURDERERS, PEDOPHILES IN HOLIDAY BLITZ DHS publicly announced Charles' deportation after Fox News obtained details of his removal, specifically referencing the viral video of Charles praising former President Joe Biden during his arrest. "This illegal alien gang member from Haiti had quite the rap sheet," DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin said in a statement, citing Charles' convictions for assault and battery on a public employee, resisting arrest and drug trafficking. Mullin also criticized the immigration policies of the Obama and Biden administrations and credited the Trump administration with carrying out Charles' removal. "Once again: if you’re here illegally, we will find you, arrest you, and remove you from the United States of America," Mullin said. HOUSE REPUBLICAN BREAKS WITH TRUMP, SAYS ENDING HAITIAN TPS RISKS US HEALTHCARE 'CRISIS' DHS said Charles had originally received Temporary Protected Status (TPS) during the Obama administration in February 2013, and was admitted to the U.S. in July of that year, according to DHS. U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services terminated his TPS in July 2022, according to DHS. The White House separately provided Fox News with a statement following Charles' deportation. "This gang member and criminal illegal alien loved Obama, Biden, and open-border Democrats who let him enter our country with TPS and allowed him to terrorize American citizens," White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis said. "Thanks to the Trump administration, he is now off our streets and back in Haiti," she continued, while contrasting Trump's immigration enforcement policies with those of Democrats. DHS also posted a tongue-in-cheek photo of President Donald Trump at his viral McDonald's campaign trail stop waving goodbye to accompany the news. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The deportation came more than a year and a half after Charles predicted the opposite as ICE officers placed him under arrest in front of Fox News cameras. "I’m not going back to Haiti," he said at the time. Charles was deported by ICE to Haiti on Thursday, DHS said.

articles.title: Democrat rebels defy Jeffries to hand GOP critical win just before midterms
articles.summary: House Democrats Jared Golden and Marie Gluesenkamp Perez broke ranks to rescue a Republican rule vote, dealing a fresh blow to Hakeem Jeffries.
articles.body: A pair of moderate House Democrats defied House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., on Tuesday, rescuing Republicans from an embarrassing final week before the November midterms. Reps. Jared Golden, D-Maine, and Marie Gluesenkamp Perez, D-Wash., voted with Republicans on a procedural hurdle known as a "rule vote," aimed at allowing the House to consider a slew of other bills this week. It’s an embarrassing blow to Jeffries’ leadership; it is almost unheard of for the minority party to break ranks and help the majority pass one of their rules, even if lawmakers on that side support the underlying legislation. LINDSEY GRAHAM'S FINAL MISSION TO PUNISH PUTIN CLEARS SENATE AFTER YEARLONG FIGHT Golden’s spokesman told Fox News Digital that the congressman’s vote was to advance a Russia sanctions bill that would have effectively been killed had the Tuesday evening rule vote failed. "Congressman Golden has been a consistent supporter of America’s allies in Ukraine. He didn’t want to see the Russia sanctions bill die in a rule vote after passing with overwhelming bipartisan support in the Senate," the spokesman said. Fox News Digital reached out to Gluesenkamp Perez’s office as well. The congresswoman posted on X, "I’m proud to represent one of the largest Ukrainian communities in America-people who have lost fathers, mothers, sons and daughters in the fight to defeat fascism. articles.title: Senate moves to rein in college sports 'Wild West' with sweeping new rules for players, schools
articles.summary: The Protect College Sports Act targets name, image and likeness (NIL) rules, transfer portal limits and a revenue sharing cap in the Senate.
articles.body: The Senate took a major first step to advancing standardized, federal guardrails on college sports as name, image and likeness (NIL) has transformed the landscape of collegiate athletics. Lawmakers moved the Protect College Sports Act, led by Sen. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, and Sen. Maria Cantwell, D-Wash., onto the next phase, opening up the opportunity for the Senate to advance the bipartisan bill later in the week. "I think most people acknowledge that the current landscape of college sports is a mess," Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., said ahead of the vote. "It needs to be addressed." SENATE ADVANCES LANDMARK PROTECT COLLEGE SPORTS ACT, IGNORING SEC AND BIG TEN OPPOSITION WITH CLOCK TICKING At its core, Cruz pitched the legislation as a means to corral the chaos that has unfolded in college athletics since the National Collegiate Athletic Association (NCAA) made its landmark decision in 2021 to allow student-athletes to benefit financially while playing collegiate football, basketball and many others. "Some have asked why should Congress get in the middle of this? The answer is simple: because Congress screwed it up in the first place," Cruz said during a press conference on Monday. "It has been the federal antitrust laws applied in litigation after litigation after litigation that have had the effect of tearing down essentially all the rules," he continued. "So right now it is the Wild West." CRUZ AND CANTWELL REFUSE TO BEND TO SEC AND BIG TEN CONCERNS IN REVISED COLLEGE ATHLETICS LEGISLATION The Protect College Sports Act would broadly add restrictions to the transfer portal for student-athletes, create a uniform eligibility framework of five years, recruiting and tampering guardrails that establish when schools or agents can contact or recruit a student-athlete, a federal standard for NIL rules, and a revenue-sharing cap. Opponents of the bill, including Sen. Chris Murphy, D-Conn., contended that the Protect College Sports Act would take away bargaining power from student-athletes and create exemptions from antitrust laws for colleges. "The ‘chaos’ is that (mostly black) athletes now have bargaining power and white coaches and sports industry execs hate it," Murphy said on X. KATIE UHLAENDER: ATHLETES RISK PAYING THE PRICE IF PROTECT COLLEGE SPORTS ACT IS PASSED And the Congressional Black Caucus, led by Rep. Yvette Clarke, D-N.Y., announced that it would not support the bill, charging in a statement that it would not support the legislation while "Black political representation is under attack across the country," following the Supreme Court’s decision on the Voting Rights Act earlier this year. "Several months ago, before the Senate ever reached this moment, the Congressional Black Caucus made clear that Congress should not rush to provide sweeping new federal protections and legal certainty to powerful athletic institutions while those same institutions remained largely silent as Black voting rights and Black political representation came under unprecedented attack," the group said. "Let me be clear, voting rights are sacred, and I will stand in that fight with anyone," she said on the Senate floor. "But I cannot agree that the way to wage it is to hold thousands of student-athletes' scholarships, health protections and future hostages to a Supreme Court decision they did not make."

articles.title: House panel votes to hold Epstein associate Leon Black in contempt
articles.summary: The move came after the House Oversight Committee accused the former Wall Street private equity investor of ignoring subpoenas in its probe of Jeffrey Epstein.
articles.body: The House Oversight Committee voted Tuesday to recommend the full House find billionaire Leon Black in contempt of Congress over his refusal to comply with subpoenas related to its probe into the late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. The bipartisan vote was unanimous, 41-0. Black, a private equity investor who had a business relationship with Epstein, voluntarily sat for a closed-door transcribed interview with the Republican-led committee in late June but left before it was over, after lawmakers complained he wasn’t answering their questions. As a result, they issued subpoenas for him to turn over more information. He didn’t show up for a later deposition the committee scheduled and sued it, seeking to block the subpoenas for his appearance and nondisclosure agreements tied to Epstein. Attorneys for Black called the committee’s action a “complete abomination” in a statement ahead of the vote called by Rep. James Comer, R-Ky., the committee chair. “This is retaliation — plain and simple,” the attorneys, Susan Estrich and Aaron Cutler, wrote. “We have the constitutional right to sue Chairman Comer and the Committee because the subpoenas issued were illegitimate, illegal and a textbook abuse of power designed to bully and destroy legal protections of private citizens.” Black is a co-founder and former head of Apollo Global Management, one of Wall Street’s most prominent investment firms. He announced he was stepping down as CEO in January 2021 after an internal review found he had paid Epstein $158 million for advice on tax and estate planning and related services from 2012 to 2017. The review found that Black wasn’t involved in Epstein’s criminal activities. Black has said he didn’t engage in any wrongdoing and “deeply” regrets his involvement with Epstein, who died in jail in 2019 awaiting trial on sex trafficking charges. Black hasn’t been accused of wrongdoing by law enforcement, and he has denied any involvement in or awareness of Epstein’s illegal activity. After the Oversight contempt recommendation, the next step would be for the House to vote on the resolution. But it’s not a guarantee. Comer told NBC News after Tuesday’s vote that he expects the House to take up the resolution on Thursday. Rep. Robert Garcia of California, the top Democrat on the committee, said “today’s a really important day for justice.” He add that the committee will “work towards a strong vote of the House in a bipartisan way to get and ensure that we get our testimony and that Leon Black faces justice for these two subpoenas.”

House expected to pass data center electricity rate bill

The House on Tuesday night is expected to pass a bill aimed at shielding Americans from increased electricity costs associated with data centers.

The bill requires states to consider taking up standards that would force tech companies to shoulder the electricity cost increases associated with large data centers but doesn’t actually require them to regulate.

The bipartisan Ratepayer Protection Act , sponsored by Reps. Kathy Castor (D-Fla.) and Gabe Evans (R-Colo) is expected to pass under a fast-track process known as suspension of the rules.

The vote comes at a moment of rising backlash to both AI itself and the data centers that power it .

The legislation describes a framework under which facilities that demand a lot of electricity, like large data centers, would be charged a rate that would cover the full cost of any additional power production or electricity infrastructure required to meet their demand so that costs do not fall on the general public.

It does not force state regulators to adopt the framework, but says states must hold a hearing on such a policy within two years of the bill’s enactment.

The bill’s supporters describe it as a solid push that could ultimately spur state-level action to protect consumers.

Critics, however, say it is toothless and may not spur significant changes at a time when AI data centers threaten to drive up electricity costs and destabilize the grid .

articles.title: Democratic defectors rescue Republicans — again
articles.summary: A pair of centrist Democrats crossed the aisle on Tuesday to help GOP leaders advance a number of bills, marking the second time this month that Democratic leaders have failed to unite their caucus against the Republicans’ messaging agenda. The defections frustrated their fellow Democrats and are sure to raise new questions about how leaders…
articles.body:
A pair of centrist Democrats crossed the aisle on Tuesday to help GOP leaders advance a number of bills, marking the second time this month that Democratic leaders have failed to unite their caucus against the Republicans’ messaging agenda.

The defections frustrated their fellow Democrats and are sure to raise new questions about how leaders are managing their caucus, especially heading into elections where they’re hoping to flip control of the House.

Reps. Jared Golden (D-Maine) and Marie Gluesenkamp Perez (D-Wash.) joined Republicans to pass a procedural rule that allows a host of proposals — including a Russian sanctions bill opposed by Democrats — to come to the floor for final votes.

The Democrats’ help was crucial in putting the rule over the top, because Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) and his leadership team were wrestling with their own internal revolt in the form of conservatives who were threatening to oppose the measure.

In the end, Johnson convinced several of those GOP holdouts to back the rule, which passed 214 to 211. Without Golden and Gluesenkamp Perez, it would have failed 212 to 213.

The defections are sure to outrage Democrats — leaders and rank-and-file members alike — who were up in arms earlier in the month after the same two Democrats helped Johnson pass a similar rule advancing a separate legislative package, which consisted mostly of GOP messaging bills designed to help Republicans keep the House in November’s midterms.

On Tuesday evening, some of those internal frustrations were already trickling out.

“It’s unfortunate, it doesn’t advance the work of the American people,” Rep. Jonathan Jackson (D-Ill.) said after the vote. “That’s two individuals that are out of step with the American people that are within our party, and so hopefully there’s a wave of new people that are coming in that can overwhelm that margin.”

After the first round of defections, House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) had called a special meeting of the Democrats’ internal rules committee to discuss potential changes — and potential disciplinary measures — designed to keep the party united on procedural votes. Some Democrats wanted to strip Golden and Gluesenkamp Perez of their committee seats.

That process fizzled with no disciplinary measures taken. (Jeffries huddled with Gluesenkamp Perez, who’s in a tough reelection contest, and said he was satisfied with the discussion. Golden is retiring).

But the centrists’ decision to defect once again is sure to renew the conversation about how to keep lone-wolf members closer in line, especially on procedural votes. And it’s likely to raise questions about whether Democratic leaders didn’t draw a harder line the first time around.

“You have to tell people. And that’s the big deal,” Rep. Juan Vargas (D-Calif.) said after the first episode. “It’s not how you vote, it’s that you tell people and be up front.”
